sourceNote: Reviewed all supplied events, E0–E2590, without tools. The transcript contains substantial transcription errors, omitted audience questions, and events spanning speaker changes. Attribution follows the recoverable exchange; U marks inseparably mixed or unclear events. Findings concern the supplied wording, without audio verification. No edited teaser replays were identifiable.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we're not in a position to assess inductively the probability that God lacks morally sufficient reasons
candidates.explanation: Unseen purposes across all history are invoked to block adverse probability judgments from apparently pointless suffering (E270–296). Cognitive limitations and the utilitarian analogy supply an actual argument (E297–321), so this is no unsupported slogan. Its protective feature is the unrestricted reach of possible hidden reasons, rather than merely acknowledging uncertainty.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: the longer we spend in eternity the more the sufferings of this life shrink
candidates.explanation: Unlimited heavenly recompense makes suffering negligible regardless of its severity: the imagined beneficiary would repeat any pain for that joy (E367–375). This explicitly protects the compatibility argument through unrestricted compensation. Craig presents it conditionally within Christian theism (E322–331, E375–377), providing a theological argument rather than substituting a catchphrase for one.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: there may be unknown Goods that God brings about that we are not even aware of
candidates.explanation: After Grayling’s reply, Craig renews the claim that judging against sufficient divine reasons is impossible in principle (E987–991). Unknown goods and unavailable comparisons extend that protection to contrary suffering. Six limitations and subsequent illustrations constitute explicit reasoning (E992–1096); the finding concerns its unrestricted protective scope, not absence of supporting argument.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: the sufferings of this life will diminish to infinitesimal proportions
candidates.explanation: This renewed compact assurance again neutralizes suffering through unlimited future happiness. Christian population figures support the preceding kingdom-growth claim (E1106–1122), but do not establish compensation. Nevertheless, eternal recompense was explicitly developed at E360–377, making this a summary of an offered theological rationale rather than an unsupported slogan.

candidates.speaker: A
candidates.quote: every opportunity taken is 12 opportunities made
candidates.explanation: Grayling uses the maxim to suggest that which opportunity one takes matters little (E2140–2142), without establishing that alternatives generally compensate equally. However, continuing decision points and enduring intentions supply surrounding reasons (E2125–2137, E2143–2154), and he concedes genuinely crucial moments (E2155–2159). Whether the maxim replaces a needed reason remains uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: overall this fits into God's master plan of building the kingdom of God
candidates.explanation: Craig declines a specific tsunami explanation but assigns disasters to a beneficial plan whose reasons may emerge centuries later (E2160–2176). This protects the plan against present contrary patterns. His subsequent account of contingencies and middle knowledge supplies the intended rationale (E2177–2209), so the affirmation summarizes an argument already offered.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: we're simply not in a position to make with any confidence
candidates.explanation: The closing renews the exclusion of adverse probability judgments and the appeal to purposes extending into eternity (E2294–2306). Those devices previously protected divine goodness through unknowable reasons and unlimited compensation. Here Craig expressly references his illustrations (E2299–2300), making this a reasoned recap, not a new unsupported slogan.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: the question is not how God can justify himself to us
candidates.explanation: The question about divine justification is redirected to the critics’ own guilt before God (E2355–2361), explicitly displacing scrutiny of God. Yet Craig announces an emotional, pastoral discussion (E2314–2323) and supplies the crucifixion narrative as its basis. Whether this reversal replaces an intellectual answer or only reframes spiritual coping is uncertain.

candidates.speaker: B
candidates.quote: God is the only solution to the problem of evil
candidates.explanation: The exclusivity claim lacks a comparison establishing that all other responses leave people without hope (E2422–2426). However, Craig may mean ultimate redemption, which he explains through eternal fellowship (E2427–2431), rather than every practical response. That unlimited future good again protects against present suffering; the preceding Mabel story illustrates coping, not exclusivity.

contrasts.speaker: A
contrasts.quote: we go by our best lights and by what's most likely in the course of our experience
contrasts.explanation: Grayling supports practical prediction with the ice-cream versus kicking example, distinguishes nearer consequences from ultimate outcomes, and repeatedly qualifies his confidence. The concise principle summarizes those reasons.

contrasts.speaker: B
contrasts.quote: if those first two premises are true it follows that evil actually serves to demonstrate the existence of God
contrasts.explanation: Craig explicitly supplies premises and a conditional inference. Grayling subsequently challenges the moral foundation at E1839–1893. Whatever the premises’ merits, the striking conclusion does not substitute for an absent argument or make disagreement itself confirming evidence.
